meta.topic: Rules for the November 1828 presidential election, 13 southern and western states
meta.caveat: Quotes were captured through an automated page reader and should be spot-checked against each URL before publication. 'Thomason' = Lisa Thomason, Jacksonian Democracy and the Electoral College, PhD diss., University of North Texas, 2001. 'Keyssar' = Alexander Keyssar, The Right to Vote, appendix tables, as reproduced on a University of Wisconsin course page. 'McPherson' = McPherson v. Blacker, 146 U.S. 1 (1892), via The Founders' Constitution (U. Chicago Press). Wikipedia is used only as a pointer.

states.electorMethodDetail: Voters chose all 24 electors on a single statewide ticket. Virginia adopted the general ticket in 1800 and kept it. Result: Jackson 26,854, Adams 12,070 (UCSB).
states.whiteMenDetail: Freehold (land ownership) required. Under the 1776 constitution the right of suffrage 'shall remain as exercised at present', i.e. set by statute. The 1785 election act (still the basis in 1828) required a male citizen aged 21+ to have a freehold estate in 25 acres with a house, or 50 acres of unimproved land, or a town lot (or part) with a house, held six months (unless inherited, etc.). No taxpaying alternative until the 1830 constitution. These rules applied to elections of the House of Delegates and Senate; the same freeholders voted for presidential electors (presumed - the elector statute itself was not checked).
states.blackMenDetail: Excluded by statute. The 1785 act limits voters to 'Every male citizen (other than free negroes or mulattoes)'. Virginia had excluded free Black men since colonial acts of 1723 (Weeks) / 1762 (Keyssar Table A.5).
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. Happersett (1875) reviewed early state constitutions and found the vote 'only bestowed upon men' everywhere except possibly New Jersey (not one of these 13 states).
states.other: Virginia's 1829-30 constitutional convention (after the 1828 election) relaxed the freehold rule to admit some leaseholders and taxpaying householders; that change took effect only from 1830.

states.notes: Freehold rule and racial exclusion are clear in the 1785 statute text. I did not find the text of the 1819 revised code to confirm word-for-word re-enactment, but the WV Archives account of the 1829 convention treats the 1785 definitions as still in force. The Library of Virginia summary gives slightly different acreage (100 acres unsettled or 25/50 with house) - that is the older 1736 act; the 1785 act's 25 improved/50 unimproved is the one in force in 1828. The WV Archives page also claims Virginia was the only state with strict freehold suffrage in 1829; that is doubtful (Rhode Island kept a freehold rule until 1842) so it is not used. The elector-selection statute's own voter-qualification wording was not checked.

states.electorMethodDetail: All 15 electors on one statewide ticket, but each elector had to live in a different electoral district (a 1828 Tarboro newspaper notice: 'fifteen electors one of whom shall actually reside within each of the electoral districts'). General ticket in use since 1816, after the legislature itself chose electors in 1812 (an unpopular law repealed afterwards). Election held Thursday 13 Nov 1828.
states.whiteMenDetail: 1776 constitution: voters for the House of Commons had to be freemen 21+, resident in the county 12 months, who 'shall have paid public taxes' (taxpaying). Voters for the state Senate also needed a 50-acre freehold in the county (property). For presidential electors I could NOT find the statute; the taxpaying (Commons) rule is the most likely one but is unverified.
states.blackMenDetail: The 1776 constitution says 'freemen' with no racial bar, and free Black men who met the same tax (and, for the Senate, freehold) rules voted until the 1835 amendments, which provided that no free Negro or free person of mixed blood 'shall vote for members of the senate or house of commons'.
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. Happersett (1875) reviewed early state constitutions and found the vote 'only bestowed upon men' everywhere except possibly New Jersey (not one of these 13 states).
states.other: The governor was chosen by the legislature until 1835. Free Black men in North Carolina could still vote in 1828 - one of few southern states (with Tennessee) where this was so.

states.notes: High confidence on the constitutional rules and on free Black voting before 1835. Medium overall because I could not find the statute saying which voters (Commons taxpayers or Senate freeholders) could vote for presidential electors; I believe it was the Commons (taxpaying) electorate but did not verify it. The 1828 newspaper lists the Jackson electors by district number, which could be misread as a district election; the same notice shows all 15 were elected together.

states.electorMethodDetail: The General Assembly chose all 11 electors (all for Jackson). There was no popular vote for president in South Carolina in 1828; the legislature kept this power through 1860.
states.whiteMenDetail: Applies to elections of the state legislature (which then chose the electors). The 1790 constitution required a 50-acre freehold or town lot, or payment of a 3-shilling tax; an 1810 amendment let every free white man 21+ (two years' state residence) vote with either a freehold or six months' residence in the election district, so no property or tax was needed in 1828.
states.blackMenDetail: Excluded. The 1790 constitution's suffrage clause is limited to 'every free white man' (Keyssar dates the exclusion in the constitution to 1790; Weeks traces the word 'white' to a 1716 colonial law).
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. Happersett (1875) reviewed early state constitutions and found the vote 'only bestowed upon men' everywhere except possibly New Jersey (not one of these 13 states).
states.other: Ordinary South Carolinians had no direct vote for president at all in 1828; their influence came only through electing state legislators.

states.electorMethodDetail: 1828 was the first time Georgia voters chose electors; the legislature had chosen them through 1824. 9 electors, Jackson 19,362 vs Adams 642 (UCSB).
states.whiteMenDetail: 1798 constitution, Art. IV sec. 1: voters must be citizens and inhabitants, 21+, who 'have paid all taxes which may have been required of them' for the year before the election, and resided six months in the county. No property requirement (dropped in 1789).
states.blackMenDetail: Excluded. The 1777 constitution limited the vote to white men (Keyssar dates the exclusion to 1777). The 1798 text does not say 'white' but requires citizenship, and free people of color were not treated as citizens: Georgia's Supreme Court (Cooper v. Savannah, 1848) said they were never recognized as citizens and were not entitled to vote for the legislature.
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. Happersett (1875) reviewed early state constitutions and found the vote 'only bestowed upon men' everywhere except possibly New Jersey (not one of these 13 states).
states.other: Under the 1798 constitution as written, the governor was elected by the legislature.

states.notes: Suffrage rule: high confidence. Elector method: medium - the switch from legislative choice (1824) to a popular general ticket (1828) is shown by Thomason and by the existence of statewide popular returns, but I did not find the Georgia statute. Wikipedia points to a Oct 1824 referendum approving popular choice of electors after 1824 (not independently verified). Black exclusion after 1789 rests on citizenship, not an explicit 'white' clause in 1798.

states.electorMethodDetail: 14 electors, all for Jackson (Jackson 39,308, Adams 31,468 per UCSB). Kentucky had used districts through 1824 and used a statewide ticket in 1828.
states.whiteMenDetail: 1799 constitution, Art. II sec. 8: every free male citizen 21+ who had resided in the state two years, or in the county or town one year, could vote. No property or tax requirement. Voting was viva voce (spoken aloud), Art. VI sec. 16.
states.blackMenDetail: Excluded by the 1799 constitution: 'every free male citizen (negroes, mulattoes, and Indians excepted)'. The 1792 constitution had no racial bar.
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. Happersett (1875) reviewed early state constitutions and found the vote 'only bestowed upon men' everywhere except possibly New Jersey (not one of these 13 states).
states.other: Voters announced their choice out loud at the polls (viva voce) rather than using a secret ballot.

states.electorMethodDetail: State divided into 11 electoral districts, one elector chosen by the voters of each district; no at-large electors. Tennessee used districts until 1832. All 11 went to Jackson (Jackson 44,293, Adams 2,240 per UCSB).
states.whiteMenDetail: 1796 constitution, Art. III sec. 1: a freeman 21+ could vote if he owned a freehold in the county, OR if he had been an inhabitant of any one county for six months before the election. Because of the residence alternative, no property or tax was required (Keyssar lists Tennessee's freehold rule 'with residency alternative').
states.blackMenDetail: The 1796 constitution says 'freeman' with no racial bar, and free Black men voted under the same rules until the 1834 constitution limited the vote to free white men (exclusion effective 1834/35).
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. Happersett (1875) reviewed early state constitutions and found the vote 'only bestowed upon men' everywhere except possibly New Jersey (not one of these 13 states).
states.other: Andrew Jackson's home state; he won about 95 percent of the popular vote.

states.notes: Some secondary sources say landowners only could vote in 1796 Tennessee (teachtnhistory.org; Tocqueville's 1832 appendix says 'he must possess some property'; Weeks says 'all freeholders'). The constitution's own text gives a six-month residence alternative, so I classify it 'none'. One site (dsi.mtsu.edu, publisher unclear) dates the Black exclusion to '1835'; the constitution was adopted 1834 and ratified March 1835. The district method is supported by McPherson and Wikipedia; I did not read the Tennessee statute.

states.electorMethodDetail: 16 electors on one statewide ticket; general ticket used since 1804. Very close: Jackson 67,596, Adams 63,453 (UCSB).
states.whiteMenDetail: 1802 constitution, Art. IV sec. 1: white male inhabitants 21+, resident one year, 'who have paid or are charged with a State or county tax'. Sec. 5: men compelled to labor on the public roads (road labor) also qualified. No property requirement.
states.blackMenDetail: Excluded by the 1802 constitution ('white male inhabitants'). Keyssar dates it 1803, the year Ohio became a state.
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. Happersett (1875) reviewed early state constitutions and found the vote 'only bestowed upon men' everywhere except possibly New Jersey (not one of these 13 states).
states.other: Ohio was the closest of these 13 states in 1828.

states.notes: Sources disagree on the elector method. McPherson v. Blacker (US Supreme Court 1892) says Indiana used districts in 1824 and 1828; Thomason's dissertation (2001), Tufts' 1824 returns and Wikipedia (citing Riker & Thornbrough 1960) all point to a statewide general ticket. I weight the later, return-based scholarship more, but I did not read the Indiana statute. McPherson may have confused Indiana with Illinois. Suffrage rule is high confidence.

states.electorMethodDetail: 3 electors, all for Jackson (Jackson 9,560, Adams 4,662 per UCSB). Illinois had used districts in 1820 and 1824 (1824 split 2 Jackson, 1 Adams); for 1828 the electors appear to have been chosen statewide.
states.whiteMenDetail: 1818 constitution, Art. II sec. 27: all white male inhabitants over 21 who had resided in the state six months before the election. No property or tax requirement, and no citizenship requirement: the Illinois Supreme Court later held that 'inhabitants' included unnaturalized immigrants.
states.blackMenDetail: Excluded by the 1818 constitution ('white male inhabitants').
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. Happersett (1875) reviewed early state constitutions and found the vote 'only bestowed upon men' everywhere except possibly New Jersey (not one of these 13 states).
states.other: Immigrants who were not yet US citizens could vote in Illinois if they had lived there six months (Spragins v. Houghton, Ill. 1840, interpreting the 1818 constitution).

states.electorMethodDetail: 3 electors on a statewide ticket (Jackson 6,763, Adams 1,581 per UCSB). General ticket in use by 1820.
states.whiteMenDetail: 1817 constitution, Art. III sec. 1: every free white male 21+, US citizen, resident one year in the state and six months in the county, who was enrolled in the militia (unless exempt), OR who had paid a state or county tax. Militia enrollment was an alternative to taxpaying, so most adult white men qualified. No property requirement.
states.blackMenDetail: Excluded by the 1817 constitution ('Every free, white male person').
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. states.electorMethodDetail: 1828 was the first popular vote for president in Louisiana; the legislature had chosen electors from 1812 through 1824. 5 electors, close result: Jackson 4,605, Adams 4,082 (UCSB).
states.whiteMenDetail: 1812 constitution (Art. II sec. 8): free white male US citizens 21+, resident one year in the county, who had paid a state tax in the six months before the election. As far as I know (not verified from the text) men who had bought land from the United States could vote without the tax. No general property requirement for voters.
states.blackMenDetail: Excluded by the 1812 constitution ('free white male'); Keyssar dates the exclusion to 1812.
states.women: No. Women could not vote in this state in 1828; the suffrage clause is limited to men (see whiteMenDetail quote). The US Supreme Court in Minor v. Happersett (1875) reviewed early state constitutions and found the vote 'only bestowed upon men' everywhere except possibly New Jersey (not one of these 13 states).

states.other: The 1820 constitution also told the legislature to pass laws keeping free Black people from moving into the state; Congress objected, and Missouri was admitted in 1821 only after promising not to enforce it (the 'second Missouri Compromise').
